brief_item.title: 用计算机体系结构视角审视多智能体LLM记忆：缓存与内存协议空白
brief_item.direction_name: Agent Cache、工具结果与记忆共享
brief_item.core_conclusion: 多智能体LLM系统正触及记忆墙，瓶颈在于语义上下文如何跨智能体存储、移动与保持一致，而非算力。作者将多智能体记忆映射到经典体系结构层级，指出当前框架（如MCP over JSON-RPC）只提供消息传递，缺乏缓存共享与内存访问协议。
brief_item.mechanism: 将多智能体记忆分三层：Agent I/O层（文本/图像/网络调用，类比设备）、Agent Cache层（压缩上下文、近期工具轨迹、短期KV/嵌入，类比L1/L2/L3）、Agent Memory层（完整对话历史、向量/图/文档存储，类比主存+存储）。区分共享内存与分布式内存两种原型，提出两项缺失协议：Agent Cache共享协议（让一个智能体的KV缓存等产物被其他智能体变换复用）与Agent内存访问协议（定义读写权限、范围、粒度，并设想agent RDMA式低时延直接远程访问，绕开消息级序列化）。
brief_item.result: 概念性贡献：明确MCP的JSON-RPC只适合上下文I/O，不能承担缓存或内存共享；DriodSpeak、Cache-to-cache已探索LLM间KV缓存共享，但尚无统一协议跨智能体共享缓存产物；Letta、Mem0支持内存内共享状态，但跨智能体读写内存的协议（权限、范围、粒度）仍缺失；无任何实现或量化测量；agent RDMA仅为开放性问题，语义制品复用前可能需变换
brief_item.boundary: 明确声明观点仍处于初步演进阶段，仅作为引发讨论的起点；无实现、无测量、无共享与分布式内存原型的量化对比；agent RDMA类比是开放问题，语义制品复用前可能需变换，RDMA语义如何映射尚不清楚。
brief_item.project_relevance: 【项目判断】方向高度相关：将智能体KV缓存与工具结果显式定位为可跨智能体共享的缓存层，直接对应跨节点/跨域KV与Agent缓存复用议题；agent RDMA式低时延远程访问与跨域记忆传输方向一致；一致性讨论（语义冲突、新鲜度依赖环境状态）关系到工具结果能否跨域安全复用。但仅为概念框架，未给出WAN场景的工程指引。

facts.title: Framing Multi-Agent LLM Memory as a Computer Architecture Problem (Agent I/O/Cache/Memory Hierarchy)
facts.event_hint: UCSD architecture group proposes computer-architecture lens for multi-agent LLM memory, identifying cache-sharing and memory-access protocol gaps
facts.problem: Multi-agent LLM systems are hitting a memory wall: as context grows (longer histories, multi-modal inputs, structured traces, customized environments), performance and scalability are limited not by compute but by how semantic context is stored, moved, and kept coherent across agents. Today's agent frameworks (e.g., MCP over JSON-RPC) only provide high-level message passing, forcing all inter-agent sharing into slow, lossy serialization with no principled cache sharing or memory access semantics.
facts.mechanism: The authors map multi-agent memory onto a classical architecture hierarchy: (1) Agent I/O Layer (audio/text/images/network calls, analogous to devices); (2) Agent Cache Layer (compressed context, recent tool-call trajectories, short-term KV cache / embeddings, analogous to L1/L2/L3); (3) Agent Memory Layer (full dialogue history, vector/graph/document stores, long-term latent storage, analogous to main memory + storage). They distinguish two base prototypes mirroring classical systems — Shared Memory (single pool, needs coherence) vs Distributed Memory (per-agent local scratchpad, needs explicit synchronization). They call out two missing protocol layers: an Agent Cache Sharing Protocol (enabling one agent's cached artifacts, e.g. KV cache per DriodSpeak/Cache-to-cache, to be transformed and reused by others) and an Agent Memory Access Protocol (defining read/write permissions, scope, granularity — document/chunk/KV-record/trace — and explicitly invoking 'agent RDMA'-like low-latency direct remote memory access without message-level serialization). The hardest open gap is multi-agent memory consistency, where state is a plan/summary/tool-trace (not a scalar), writes can be speculative, conflicts are semantic contradictions, and freshness depends on environment state.

evidence.claim: MCP largely uses JSON-RPC and is best viewed as a protocol for agent context I/O (request/response, tool invocation, structured messages), not for cache or memory sharing.
Existing studies DriodSpeak and Cache-to-cache explored KV cache sharing between LLMs, but no principled unified protocol exists for sharing cached artifacts across agents.
evidence.source_locator: Section 'Missing Piece 1: Agent Cache Sharing Protocol'

evidence.claim: Frameworks like Letta and Mem0 support shared state within agent memory, but a protocol defining how agents read/write each other's memory (permissions, scope, granularity) is missing.
evidence.source_locator: Section 'Missing Piece 2: Agent Memory Access Protocol'

evidence.claim: The authors pose whether 'agent RDMA'-like patterns — low-latency direct access to remote memory without expensive message-level serialization — can be supported.

Agent consistency is harder than hardware consistency because state is a plan/summary/retrieval result/tool trace, writes may be speculative or wrong, conflicts are semantic contradictions, and freshness depends on environment state (repo version, API results, permissions).

facts.evaluation_context: This is a vision/perspective blog post (SIGARCH Computer Architecture Today blog), not a measured system. No benchmarks, hardware, or deployment scale are reported. The authors reference their own prior multi-agent frameworks (OrcaLoca for issue localization, MAGE for RTL design, Pro-V for RTL verification, PettingLLMs for multi-agent RL training) as motivating experience. Context benchmarks cited include RULER, LongBench, MMMU, VideoMME, Spider, BIRD, SWE-bench, Multi-SWE-bench, WebArena, OSWorld.
facts.limitations: Explicitly preliminary: the authors state 'our perspectives are still preliminary and evolving' and intend the post as 'a starting point to ignite a broader conversation.' No implementation, no measurements, no quantitative comparison of shared vs distributed memory prototypes. The proposed I/O/Cache/Memory hierarchy and the cache-sharing/memory-access protocols are conceptual mappings, not specified protocols. Inference: the 'agent RDMA' analogy is posed as an open question, not a design — it is unclear how RDMA semantics would map to semantic artifacts that may require transformation before reuse.
facts.project_relevance: Highly relevant to the cross-region / agent-cache direction. The explicit framing of agent KV cache and tool-result artifacts as a cache layer that should be shareable across agents directly maps to the briefing interest in KVCache cross-node/cross-region transfer and Agent cache reuse. The call for an Agent Memory Access Protocol with 'agent RDMA'-like direct remote access is conceptually aligned with low-latency cross-domain memory transfer. The consistency discussion (semantic conflicts, freshness tied to environment state) is relevant to whether tool results and memory can be safely reused across regions. However, the post provides only a conceptual frame, not engineering guidance for WAN scenarios.
source_notes: Primary source is the original SIGARCH blog post by Zhongming Yu and Jishen Zhao (UCSD), published 2026-01-20. Full text (11276 chars) was retrieved.
Document type: expert perspective/vision blog, not an empirical paper — quality score reflects full-text availability but absence of measurements.
